title: Xi Jinping Heads to Pyongyang on Monday. India Is Reading the Room.
excerpt: China's president will make his first visit to North Korea in seven years. Kim Jong Un has been flexing nuclear muscle all week. For New Delhi, the summit reshapes the security math across Asia.
body:
Chinese President Xi Jinping will arrive in Pyongyang on Monday for a two-day state visit — his first to North Korea in nearly seven years. The summit with Kim Jong Un comes after weeks of careful choreography by both sides, and it carries implications that reach well beyond the Korean Peninsula.

For India, a country that shares a contested border with China and watches the Asian power balance with forensic attention, the Xi-Kim summit is another data point in a shifting strategic landscape.

## Kim Has Spent the Week Flexing

North Korea has used the run-up to Xi's arrival to project strength in ways that would have been unthinkable during their last meeting in 2019.

On Saturday, Kim boarded the Kang Kyon, a 5,000-tonne destroyer capable of carrying nuclear-armed cruise missiles. The warship had suffered an embarrassing launch failure last year — its hull was crushed when it slipped off its cradle prematurely — but Kim declared it operational and announced plans for an even larger 10,000-tonne destroyer class.

On Sunday, Kim Yo Jong, the North Korean leader's powerful sister, issued a statement through state media reaffirming Pyongyang's status as a nuclear-armed state. She dismissed American claims that Xi and Trump had agreed on denuclearisation goals during their May summit in Beijing. "We have the most accurate information" on what was discussed, she said, without elaborating.

Earlier in the week, North Korea unveiled a new uranium-enrichment facility, with Kim calling for an "exponential" expansion of his country's nuclear arsenal. Analysts say the timing was deliberate — a signal to both Beijing and Washington that Pyongyang's nuclear programme is not on the table.

## Why China Wants This Summit

Xi's visit is, at its core, about reclaiming influence. North Korea is China's only formal treaty ally, bound by a 1961 mutual defence pact. But in recent years, Kim has tilted sharply toward Moscow — sending troops and weapons to support Russia's war in Ukraine, deepening military cooperation, and building a relationship that has made Beijing visibly uncomfortable.

China has responded with a patient courtship. Xi hosted Kim at a military parade in Beijing last year. Passenger rail and air services between the two countries have resumed. Trade, which collapsed during North Korea's pandemic-era border closures, is being rebuilt.

But the visit is not just about sentiment. For Beijing, a stable and aligned North Korea serves as a buffer between Chinese territory and the 28,500 American troops stationed in South Korea. Losing Pyongyang to Russia's orbit would weaken China's leverage across Northeast Asia at precisely the moment it is competing with the United States for regional primacy.

"Having Xi visit Pyongyang is a big deal and the culmination of a good couple of comeback years for Kim," said Andrew Gilholm, an analyst at Control Risks.

## What India Is Watching

New Delhi does not have a direct stake in Korean Peninsula politics, but the Xi-Kim summit matters for at least three reasons.

First, any deepening of the China-North Korea axis adds another variable to India's northern security calculus. China already maintains a significant military presence along the Line of Actual Control. A more stable China-North Korea relationship frees up Chinese strategic bandwidth — bandwidth that could be redirected toward other fronts, including the Indian border.

Second, the nuclear dimension. North Korea's expanding arsenal sets a precedent for nuclear proliferation across Asia. India, itself a nuclear-armed state outside the Non-Proliferation Treaty, has long argued that its deterrent is defensive. But a Northeast Asia where nuclear capabilities are being expanded exponentially makes the regional security environment more volatile for everyone.

Third, the Russia factor. India has maintained a delicate balancing act with Moscow — buying Russian oil at a premium, abstaining from Western censure of the Ukraine war, while simultaneously deepening defence ties with the United States. A stronger China-North Korea-Russia triangle complicates that balance. If Beijing succeeds in pulling Pyongyang partly away from Moscow, it could reshape the trilateral dynamic in ways that either ease or intensify pressure on India's own diplomatic positioning.

## The Optics and the Substance

In 2019, Kim gave Xi a lavish reception: thousands of North Koreans held up placards forming Xi's face and the Chinese flag, while a choir performed "I Love Thee, China." This time, the optics are likely to be equally grand but the substance more transactional.

China wants economic cooperation — expanded tourism, trade, and infrastructure. North Korea wants security guarantees and sanctions relief. Neither side is expected to make concessions on the nuclear programme.

For India, which held ten bilateral defence meetings at the Shangri-La Dialogue just last week and is weeks away from finalising its first tranche of a trade deal with the United States, the Xi-Kim summit is a reminder that Asia's security architecture is being quietly renegotiated — and that India needs to be at every table where the terms are being set.
